The Unseen Thread

National Artist Arturo Luz  •  GAMABA Artist Lang Dulay

Why these artistsNational Artist: LuzGAMABA Artist: DulayThe CuratorsShare
Curatorial Statement
Fun fact: why "The Unseen Thread"?
It has two meanings. Unseen: at first glance, the meaning behind Arturo Luz's abstract pieces is hard to see, because his ideas hide inside lines, shapes and empty space. Thread: Lang Dulay's art is woven from abaca thread, with T'nalak designs that came to her in dreams. Both artists ask us to look closer, and a thread of Filipino identity runs through the work of each.

Why These Two Artists?

Our team reached consensus (discussion documented on the SB Class Group page) to pair a modernist painter from the city with an indigenous master weaver from Lake Sebu. Both reduce the world into line, shape, and repeating pattern, yet they come from very different Philippine histories.

Selection criteria: (1) national recognition: Luz was named National Artist in 1997 and Dulay received the GAMABA in 1998, both under President Fidel V. Ramos; (2) historical significance: Luz shaped postwar Philippine modernism and its museums, while Dulay safeguarded the T'boli T'nalak tradition; (3) diversity: painting, sculpture and mural beside woven textile; (4) strong visual material for aesthetic analysis.

National Artist

Arturo Luz (1926–2021)

Born in Lipa, Batangas, Luz trained at the University of Santo Tomas, then in California, Brooklyn and Paris. He founded The Luz Gallery in 1960, served as founding director of the Metropolitan Museum of Manila (1976–1986), and was conferred National Artist in 1997 (Proclamation No. 1007). His work is known for austere, economical use of line, color and space.

1926 Born in Lipa, Batangas

1950s Studies abroad; early Carnival series

1960 Opens The Luz Gallery

1976–86 Founding director, Metropolitan Museum of Manila

1997 Named National Artist

2021 Passes away at 94

GAMABA Artist

Lang Dulay (1928–2015), "The Dreamweaver"

A T'boli princess from Lake Sebu, South Cotabato, Lang Dulay began learning T'nalak weaving at 12 from her mother, Luan Senig. She resisted synthetic materials, keeping to pure abaca fiber and natural plant dyes. Her designs came from dreams she believed were gifts from Fa Dula, the T'boli goddess of abaca. She held a mental repertoire of about 100 motifs.

1928 Born in Lake Sebu

1940 Begins weaving at age 12

1998 Receives the GAMABA; her work is shown at the Smithsonian for the Philippine Independence Centennial

Later years Founds the Manlilikha ng Bayan Center to teach her granddaughters and community

2015 Passes away at 86
